name: The AI Enablement Audit
title: The AI Enablement Audit
answer: The AI Enablement Audit is a structured review of how an organisation adopts, deploys and governs artificial intelligence across its business functions. It sits within AI security auditing and enterprise enablement, and it looks at both the technical estate and the human and procedural layers around it. The audit typically covers model and tool inventory, data flows, access controls, vendor arrangements, staff training and internal policy. Its purpose is to establish what is actually in use, how it is governed, and where the gaps sit between stated policy and daily practice.

AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit is a structured review of how an organisation adopts, deploys and governs artificial intelligence across its business functions. It sits within AI security auditing and enterprise enablement, and it looks at both the technical estate and the human and procedural layers around it. The audit typically covers model and tool inventory, data flows, access controls, vendor arrangements, staff training and internal policy. Its purpose is to establish what is actually in use, how it is governed, and where the gaps sit between stated policy and daily practice.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the organisation's existing systems rather than a single dedicated platform. Evidence is drawn from identity and access management, cloud and endpoint logs, software asset registers, procurement records, data catalogues and model registries where these exist. Questionnaires, interviews and configuration reviews fill in what the logs cannot show, particularly for staff using public AI tools outside approved channels. The output is usually held in a findings register or governance platform that links each observation to an owner and a remediation date.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with scoping, agreeing which business units, systems and AI use cases fall inside the review. Auditors then collect evidence through document review, technical inspection, interviews and, where appropriate, controlled testing of access and data handling. Findings are assessed against the organisation's own policies and against recognised frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework or ISO/IEC 42001. Each finding is rated for likelihood and impact, assigned to an owner, and tracked to closure. The audit is repeated or refreshed as new models, tools and use cases enter the estate.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The audit produces a record of what was examined, when, by whom, and on what evidence, which matters when regulators, customers or insurers ask how AI is controlled. Provenance of models, training data and third party components is documented so that origin and licensing can be traced. Personal data, confidential material and intellectual property handled by AI systems are mapped to the lawful basis and contractual terms that cover them. Findings and remediation status are reported to an accountable owner, often a risk committee or board level function, and retained for the period the organisation's records policy requires.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expectation is shifting from one off reviews toward continuous monitoring, with automated checks feeding a live view of AI use across the estate. Regulatory pressure, including obligations on general purpose AI under the EU AI Act and sector rules from financial and health regulators, is pushing audits from voluntary good practice toward documented evidence of control. Agentic systems that act with limited human oversight raise new questions about authority, logging and rollback that current audit methods only partly address. The practical direction is toward audits that are repeatable, evidence linked and fast enough to keep pace with how quickly AI tools enter the workplace.
